content: The report outlines the process of monitoring and analyzing cohorts of patients starting antiretroviral therapy (ART) at specific time intervals. For each cohort, data is collected at baseline (the time of ART initiation) and then at subsequent intervals, such as 6 months, 12 months, 24 months, and beyond. The analysis tracks patient outcomes, including those who remain on first-line, second-line, or third-line ART regimens, as well as those who stop treatment, are lost to follow-up, or die. At baseline, the number of patients starting ART at a facility is recorded as the original cohort. Over time, the cohort is adjusted to account for patients transferring into the facility (transfer-ins) and those transferring out (transfer-outs). The net current cohort is calculated by adding transfer-ins and subtracting transfer-outs from the original cohort. This adjusted cohort is used to monitor outcomes over time. Patients are categorized based on their treatment regimens. Those on first-line regimens are recorded in a specific column, and any switches to second-line or third-line regimens are documented accordingly. For example, if a patient switches from a first-line to a second-line regimen, this is noted in the second-line column. If the patient later switches to a third-line regimen, only the most recent change is recorded to avoid double-counting. The report also tracks patients who stop treatment, die, or are lost to follow-up (LTF). At baseline, these categories are not applicable, but they are recorded in subsequent intervals. For example, if a patient is lost to follow-up at 4 months but returns at 8 months, they are recorded as restart and included in the appropriate treatment category. Viral load (VL) testing is another critical component of the analysis. The number of patients who receive a VL test result is recorded, as well as the number of those with suppressed viral loads (defined as <1000 copies/mL). The percentage of the cohort alive and on ART with VL suppression is calculated, along with the percentage of those who received VL results and achieved suppression. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using ART cards and registers in maternal and child health settings. Retention rates for these patients can be disaggregated by time intervals (e.g., 0, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months) to monitor outcomes. The cohort analysis is conducted on a monthly or quarterly basis, with data summarized from the ART register. Long-term cohort analysis may also be performed at the facility level, tracking outcomes over multiple years (e.g., 2, 3, or 5 years). This allows for retrospective data entry and comprehensive monitoring of patient outcomes. In summary, the cohort analysis process involves systematic data collection and monitoring of ART outcomes, including retention, regimen changes, viral load suppression, and patient transfers.
